The vulnerability assigned to this CVE is in Chromium Open Source Software (OSS) which is consumed by Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based). It is being documented in the Security Update Guide to announce that the latest version of Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) is no longer vulnerable.

How can I see the version of the browser?

  1. In your Microsoft Edge browser, click on the 3 dots (...) on the very right-hand side of the window
  2. Click on Help and Feedback
  3. Click on About Microsoft Edge

factors.applicability: Microsoft Customer Action Required: Yes for Edge (Chromium-based), product 22414.
factors.exploitability: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R. Social engineering and a crafted HTML page are required, with user interaction.
factors.remediation_context: Standard Important-tier remediation. The Edge update is the remediation. Chrome CNA rates Low against Microsoft Important (scale divergence).
factors.technical_impact: Microsoft C:H/I:H/A:H. CNA impact is a web origin policy bypass, which is a security-feature bypass.
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft exploitability unknown, so Plausible pending other evidence. KEV false, exploitation_detected false, EPSS 0.00259. CISA-ADP SSVC exploitation none.
factors.uncertainty: Chrome CNA severity Low against Microsoft Important. Public exploit maturity is not published. Whether the CORS bypass yields data disclosure is not stated, so no disclosure tag is applied.
factors.workload_context: Browser client endpoints. No concentration is stated and is unknown.

risk_communication.summary: Edge CORS origin-policy bypass via a social-engineered HTML page. Microsoft Important 8.8, UI:R, EPSS 0.00259, no KEV. Scheduled.
risk_communication.why_this_action: Important with Plausible likelihood does not meet the Elevated archetype. The standard Scheduled action applies, and social engineering with user interaction limits exposure.
risk_communication.control_limitations: Only the web content-filtering route earns one step. Browser ACLs and CORS policy are not credited, and no exact block exists.
reassessment_triggers: KEV listing or exploitation detected
Public exploit or exploit-maturity signal
EPSS reaching 0.01 or 0.10
Microsoft revision changing CVSS or exploitability
Clarification of the disclosure impact

tag_evidence.evidence: Chrome CNA: 'to bypass web origin policy' in CORS.
Chrome CNA: 'via a crafted HTML page'.
Attacker HTML page the victim renders after social engineering (Chrome CNA).

attack_path.evidence: Chrome CNA: a remote attacker leveraging social engineering bypasses web origin policy in CORS via a crafted HTML page. The victim's browser renders the attacker page, so this is outbound client web delivery. No inbound listener is established.

cna.description: Incorrect authorization in CORS in Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.38 allowed a remote attacker leveraging social engineering to bypass web origin policy via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: Low)

Successful exploitation could allow an extension to be installed and run despite an administrator's extension allowlist policy. The user must be convinced to install the extension.

Why is the attack complexity rated High?

Successful exploitation through the extension marketplace requires the attacker to control a publishing identity that meets specific conditions. Obtaining that identity is a prerequisite beyond simply creating a malicious extension.

According to the CVSS metrics, successful exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to major loss of confidentiality (C:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

This vulnerability discloses a user's NTLMv2 hash to the attacker who could use this to authenticate as the user.

External attackers could send specially crafted emails that will cause a connection from the victim to an untrusted location of attackers' control. notes.title: Description
notes.value: Weak authentication in Windows Kerberos allows an authorized attacker to elevate privileges over a network.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who controls authentication in a trusted forest could send specially crafted authentication information to the target forest. Successful exploitation could raise the integrity level of the attacker's identity to System, allowing actions otherwise blocked by integrity-level restrictions where existing resource permissions already allow access. This does not grant SYSTEM-account privileges or target-forest administrator membership.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation requires an existing trust relationship between the attacker's forest and the target forest, together with resource permissions that already allow the attacker's identity access. The vulnerability bypasses integrity-level restrictions but does not grant otherwise absent resource access permissions.

notes.title: Description
notes.value: Server-side request forgery (ssrf) in Microsoft Office SharePoint allows an authorized attacker to disclose information over a network.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An authenticated attacker with Manage Lists permissions could send a specially crafted SOAP request to an affected SharePoint server that causes the server to connect to an attacker-selected internal or external destination and return the response. On a domain-joined farm, the outbound request may also use the SharePoint server's Windows identity. No additional user interaction is required.

notes.value:

No, the Preview Pane is not an attack vector.

factors.remediation_context: Security update 5002945 is published. No workaround is stated.
factors.technical_impact: High confidentiality impact, with no integrity or availability impact. The SSRF can return responses from internal or external destinations and may use the server's Windows identity on a domain-joined farm.
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft exploitation assessment is less-likely (Plausible). KEV false, exploitation not detected, publicly disclosed false, EPSS null. CNA record has no ADP SSVC.
factors.uncertainty: Microsoft severity is Important while CNA cvss-qualitative band is MEDIUM from the 6.5 score; the vendor basis is retained. Internal targets reachable from the server are unknown.
factors.workload_context: SharePoint Server Subscription Edition, a shared collaboration workload. The outbound request may carry the server's domain identity, which concentrates exposure in the service account. Scheduled is challenged on that concentration but the PR:L Manage Lists prerequisite and Plausible rating keep it at Scheduled.

risk_communication.summary: Important SharePoint SSRF that discloses responses from attacker-selected destinations. Requires a Manage Lists account and no user interaction.
risk_communication.why_this_action: Standard-remediation archetype. Scheduled is challenged: an SSRF from a domain-joined farm can reach internal services under the server's identity, but the Plausible rating and authenticated prerequisite do not justify Out-of-cycle on current evidence.
risk_communication.control_limitations: Credits are ordinary inbound benefits. Permitted internal peers and existing Manage Lists holders remain residual. Egress restriction is not credited here.

Source gives only update guidance and no workaround text. No credit.
No CVE-specific or exploit-specific signature is cited for the SQL Server TDS path. No credit.
WAF inspects HTTP requests to a web route. The source describes authenticated SQL Server network access, not a web route.
No setting that removes the uninitialized-memory prerequisite is named. Encryption enforcement would not remove an authorized read of process memory. No credit.
Authentication already gates the path (PR:L). Strong authentication does not cure a flaw reachable by a valid login, so no credit.

No ASR technique maps to uninitialized-resource disclosure. No credit.
No user-delivered content route is established. The path is authenticated network access.
No Office document path.
No tested prevention rule for this memory disclosure is cited. Generic EDR presence earns no credit.
Detection and response only. No likelihood or consequence credit.
The impact is confidentiality, which backups do not address. No credit.

Strong isolation of the SQL entry path from untrusted networks removes the external network opportunity. Authorized peers inside the boundary remain residual. Ordinary single band, overlapping network reachability and capped by the engine.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metrics, successful exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to major loss of confidentiality (C:H), but lead to no loss of integrity (I:N) or availability (A:N). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

The Confidentiality is set to High because an attacker who successfully exploits this vulnerability could access tokens beyond a user’s typical privilege.

The exploit results in token disclosure, however it does not affect the Integrity and Availability of the system. Thus, both of these are set as None.

notes.title: Description
notes.value: Improper verification of cryptographic signature in JDBC Driver for SQL Server allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass a security feature over a network.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who controls or can impersonate the SQL Server could replay a legitimate attestation response while substituting attacker-controlled key material during a client connection. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to obtain column encryption keys and access or modify protected database data.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation requires Always Encrypted with secure enclaves to use HGS attestation. The attacker must also control or impersonate the SQL Server connection and have access to a legitimate attestation response that can be replayed.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
What could an attacker accomplish by exploiting this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to bypass secure-enclave attestation, obtain column encryption keys, decrypt protected database data, and create modified encrypted data that the client accepts as valid.

No Microsoft technique-specific ASR rule maps to a DHCP packet use-after-free in the source. Generic ASR presence is not credited.
Detection on the DHCP host can alert after exploitation but does not lower exploitation likelihood or consequence under the framework.
No tested endpoint prevention rule for this use-after-free is established in the source. Generic EDR presence gives no credit.
Delivery is a crafted network packet to a listening DHCP service, not user-delivered content, so no content-delivery path exists for this control.
Inbound network direction is applicable, but no CVE-specific or exploit-specific IPS signature is named in the source. Generic IPS presence is not credited.

Recovery capability does not reduce exploitation likelihood. The source impact is confidentiality, integrity and availability; backups do not contain confidentiality or integrity compromise, so no consequence credit.

Inbound network entry is applicable, but the DHCP service must answer clients on its segment. Full isolation would also remove legitimate service and overlaps the segmentation credit; no separate supported marginal removal is established, so no credit.
PR:N means no privilege is required, so there is no removable required privilege. The DHCP service account's rights and any containment are not stated in the source. No credit.
No Office document or user-delivered content route is involved; the entry is a network packet.
No DHCP setting is named in the source that directly removes the use-after-free prerequisite. No credit.

Established inbound route: crafted packets to the DHCP listener. Removing public ingress gives ordinary benefit without proof of customer exposure. Residual: DHCP clients and relays on permitted local or internal paths remain reachable, so no path block.

Restrictive ACLs on the DHCP UDP service restrict attacker-sourced packets to permitted client, relay and management peers. Residual: permitted DHCP clients and relays keep the entry path. Overlaps external-exposure removal but has its own internal benefit.

The named DHCP Server role is the request-handling listener that the exploit reaches. Disabling it on hosts where it is not needed removes the required operation. Residual: hosts still running the role remain exposed. No vendor-disable text is claimed, so no strong exact-path credit.
CVSS PR:N and the FAQ state no authentication gate, so authentication cannot gate the vulnerable path.
Microsoft lists only security updates (KB5131085, KB5131090, KB5131080, KB5131077, KB5131291). No workaround text is present.
DHCP is not an HTTP request path, so a WAF cannot inspect or block this route.

cna.description: ntopng is a web-based network traffic monitoring application. Prior to 6.7.260717, scripts/lua/rest/v2/add/host/to_scan.lua and scripts/lua/rest/v2/exec/host/schedule_vulnerability_scan.lua accept scan_ports from any authenticated session, including non-administrator users, while deployments with login disabled expose the same request without authentication. The endpoints validate scan_ports with validateSingleWord, which permits shell metacharacters, and persist the value for the minute vulnerability-scan scheduler. The scheduler concatenates the value into an nmap command through nmap_scan_host and executes it through ntop.execCmd or ntop.execCmdAsync using popen. For the tcp_portscan and cve modules, a preliminary nmap -sn probe must first report the target as up before the attacker-controlled ports are used. When nmap is installed, this command injection allows arbitrary operating-system commands to execute as the ntopng service account without further user interaction. This issue is fixed in version 6.7.260717.

notes.value:
I am running SQL Server on my system. What action do I need to take?

Update your relevant version of SQL Server using the applicable November 2026 security update listed below.

There are GDR and/or CU (Cumulative Update) updates offered for my version of SQL Server. How do I know which update to use?

  • First, determine your SQL Server version number. For more information, see Microsoft Knowledge Base Article 321185 - How to determine the version, edition, and update level of SQL Server and its components.
  • Second, locate the range containing your current version number in the following table. The corresponding update is the one you need to install.

Note: If your version is not represented in the table, review the applicable update's prerequisites and the support status of your SQL Server release before choosing an update. Absence from this table alone does not establish that a version is unsupported.

General Distribution Release (GDR) updates provide security and other broadly applicable critical fixes. Cumulative Updates (CUs) include accumulated fixes for the applicable SQL Server release. I am running SharePoint Server 2016. Do the updates for SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016 also apply to the version I am running?

Yes. The same KB number applies to both SharePoint Server 2016 and SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016. Customers running either version should install the security update to be protected from this vulnerability.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to run script in the security context of the affected SharePoint user and perform actions permitted to that user.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An authenticated attacker with permissions to add or modify content on an affected SharePoint page could store malicious script content in the page. The script could run in the security context of another user when that user views and interacts with the affected content, potentially allowing the attacker to access or modify SharePoint data available to that user.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who controls a malicious NFS server could send specially crafted responses to an affected Windows Client for NFS system connected to that server. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to gain SYSTEM privileges on the client system.

factors.applicability: Microsoft Customer Action Required is Yes. Affected products include Windows 10 1607/1809/21H2/22H2, Windows 11 23H2 through 26H2, and Windows Server 2016 through 2025. MSRC remediation product IDs are used as the applicability source.
factors.exploitability: Attacker must control an NFS server that a victim client connects to, and must win a race (AC:H). PR:N and UI:N. No stated user action. Microsoft publisher exploit maturity is E:U.
factors.remediation_context: Security updates are listed per product (KB5131291, KB5131085, KB5131096, KB5131090, KB5131087, KB5132061/KB5132043, KB5131080/KB5131077, KB5132059). No workaround or service-disablement guidance is in the record.
factors.technical_impact: Two source claims are preserved and conflict. The MSRC title, description and FAQ state elevation of privilege to SYSTEM. The MSRC CVRF impact entries list 'Remote Code Execution' for every product ID. The CNA record gives CWE-416 only. CVSS C:H/I:H/A:H is unchanged. The conflict is not resolved here and does not change the CVSS or the archetype.
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft exploitation_assessment is less-likely (Plausible floor). KEV false. Exploitation detected false. Publicly disclosed false. EPSS null, which is unavailable, not a low score. CVE Program SSVC null.
factors.uncertainty: Unresolved RCE versus EoP conflict. The route by which a victim is steered to the attacker NFS server is not stated. NFS transport and port are not stated. Client process privilege context is unknown. No EPSS value and no workaround. MSRC and CNA product lists are not fully identical, so MSRC product IDs are used for applicability.
factors.workload_context: Windows Client for NFS is a file-sharing client consumed by workstations and servers. Product coverage spans endpoint and server SKUs. How many hosts connect to external NFS servers and how concentrated the SYSTEM result would be is unknown and not inferred.

risk_communication.summary: Important, CVSS 8.1 NFS client use-after-free giving SYSTEM from an attacker-controlled NFS server. Race-dependent (AC:H). Microsoft rates exploitation less likely, with no KEV, no detected exploitation, no public disclosure, and no EPSS value. Patch within the standard scheduled cycle, with review of the RCE versus EoP conflict.
risk_communication.why_this_action: Standard-remediation baseline is Scheduled. No floor raises it: the Critical RCE archetype needs CVSS 9.0 or higher, and Elevated-high needs Elevated likelihood, which Microsoft does not assign here. Impact is high (SYSTEM, C/I/A High) and Customer Action Required is Yes, so the action stays Scheduled rather than being discounted. Preserved RCE impact claims are a reason for review, not an automatic escalation.
risk_communication.control_limitations: No workaround or disablement text in the source. Egress ACL and isolation credit is one step each and leaves permitted or compromised NFS peers in place. No exploit-specific IPS, EDR prevention, or application-control credit is established. Patching is the primary control.

No inbound path inferred.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tipc: protect node reset trace dump with node lock

The tipc_node_reset_links trace event asks tipc_node_dump() to walk the
node's link entries. Unlike the other node events that request link data,
this event runs without the node lock.

This permits bearer teardown to free a link while the trace callback is
dumping it:

  CPU 0                                CPU 1
  trace_tipc_node_reset_links()
    tipc_node_dump()
      l = n->links[0].link
                                       tipc_node_write_lock()
                                       kfree(l)
                                       n->links[0].link = NULL
                                       tipc_node_write_unlock()
      tipc_link_dump(l)

tipc_link_dump() then dereferences the stale pointer. KASAN reported:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in tipc_link_dump
  Read of size 4 by task poc/115
  Call Trace:
   tipc_link_dump+0x10cb/0x16b0
   tipc_node_dump+0x4bb/0x740
   trace_event_raw_event_tipc_node_class+0x258/0x360
   tipc_node_reset_links+0x14d/0x1a0
   tipc_rcv+0x13f5/0x3030
   tipc_udp_recv+0x4e3/0x670
  Allocated by task 0:
   tipc_link_create+0x1e1/0x1020
   tipc_node_check_dest+0x7d2/0x11a0
   tipc_disc_rcv+0xdbf/0x1430
  Freed by task 89:
   kfree+0x131/0x3c0
   tipc_node_link_down+0x267/0x4b0
   tipc_node_delete_links+0xec/0x160
   bearer_disable+0x107/0x260

Take the node write lock around the trace event. This serializes the
dump against tipc_node_link_down(delete=true), which frees the link
under the same write lock.

title: tcp: Fix potential UAF in reqsk_timer_handler().

mitigation_candidates.evidence: Inbound TCP handshake to a listening kernel socket is the source-established entry route, so public-ingress removal has ordinary marginal benefit without proof of customer exposure. Residual: internal or permitted peers that can still send handshake segments. No exact block: the migration-path prerequisite and BPF alternative remain.

Restrictive ACLs on TCP ingress to the listening service restrict the source-established inbound handshake path. Residual: allowed internal peers and permitted sources can still deliver the SYN/ACK sequence. Overlap with public-ingress removal is capped by the engine, not by this assessment.

The required operation is kernel TCP handshake processing on listeners, which cannot be disabled as a service. The vulnerable branch depends on the optional SO_REUSEPORT migration feature, and disabling an optional feature is an optionality claim with no vendor disablement text in the source. No ordinary credit here; the prerequisite is credited under protocol_hardening instead.

Source (Microsoft remediations) gives only a Security Update and Azure Linux upgrade Release Notes; no CVE-specific workaround text exists. A Release Notes entry is not mitigation text, so zero effect.

Inbound network route is applicable, but no CVE-specific or exploit-specific IPS signature in prevention mode is evidenced in the source. Generic IPS presence is not credit. Low confidence, zero effect.

The vulnerable path is the TCP handshake below any application request layer; a WAF inspects HTTP requests to a protected service and does not cover this route or provide a tested blocking rule for it.

CNA scenario states the buggy path runs only when net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req is non-default (default 0) or a BPF migration program is present. Setting that sysctl to its default removes the sysctl prerequisite. Credit assumes it is at default across the selected scope; the BPF migration alternative remains residual, so one step only and no exact block.
CVSS PR:N and CNA scenario: the SYN is accepted in tcp_conn_request() before accept() and before any credential check. No authentication gates the vulnerable path, so no identity gating credit.
PR:N: the attacker needs no privilege. No specific removable privilege is required, and post-exploit containment is not source-established as a consequence reduction.
The exploit chain is network handshake traffic processed by the kernel; it does not depend on starting an untrusted executable or script on the target.
No ASR technique rule maps to a remote kernel TCP timer use-after-free; no enforced rule is evidenced.
No user-delivered content route is established; the trigger is network handshake traffic with no user action.
No Office or document content route is established by the source.
Kernel-level exploit prevention would be needed; no tested prevention rule for this UAF behavior is evidenced. Generic EDR presence is not credit.
Detection and response coverage improves crash or compromise visibility only; it provides no likelihood credit under the catalogue rule.

Backups provide no likelihood credit. Source impact is C:H and I:H with a kernel panic on A:H; backups do not contain confidentiality or integrity compromise, and recovery is not containment, so consequence credit is zero.

Strong isolation of the inbound TCP entry path is a network mechanism that removes opportunity for remote handshake delivery. Residual: peers permitted inside the isolation boundary can still deliver segments. Ordinary single step only; not an exact vendor block.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tcp: Fix potential UAF in reqsk_timer_handler().

When TCP socket migration fails at inet_ehash_insert() in
reqsk_timer_handler(), we jump to the no_ownership: label
and free the new reqsk immediately with __reqsk_free().

Thus, we must stop the new reqsk's timer before jumping to the
label, but the timer might be missed since the cited commit,
resulting in UAF.

As we are in the original reqsk's timer context, we can safely
call timer_delete_sync() for the new reqsk.

Let's pass false to __inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop() to stop
the new reqsk's timer.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xen-netback: defer xenvif_mcast_addr_list_free()

In order for the function to legitimately avoid locking/RCU, it needs to
run after all TX/RX processing has finished/stopped: Lookups happen from
xenvif_start_xmit(), while adds/removes happen from xenvif_tx_action()
(called out of xenvif_poll()).

Move the call out of xenvif_disconnect_data() (the call to the function
from connect()'s error path doesn't require any cleaning up there), and
put it past the synchronization point in backend_disconnect().

This is XSA-527 / CVE-2026-100081.

notes.value:
An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists when reparse points are created by sandboxed processes allowing sandbox escape. An attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability could use the sandbox escape to elevate privileges on an affected system.

To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker would first have to log on to the system, and then run a specially crafted application to take control over the affected system.

The security update addresses the vulnerability by preventing sandboxed processes from creating reparse points targeting inaccessible files.

notes.title: Description
notes.value:
An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists in the Windows Installer when the Windows Installer fails to properly sanitize input leading to an insecure library loading behavior.

A locally authenticated attacker could run arbitrary code with elevated system privileges. An attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights.

The security update addresses the vulnerability by correcting the input sanitization error to preclude unintended elevation.

notes.title: Description
notes.value:
An elevation of privilege vulnerability exists in the Windows Installer when the Windows Installer fails to properly sanitize input leading to an insecure library loading behavior.

A locally authenticated attacker could run arbitrary code with elevated system privileges. An attacker could then install programs; view, change, or delete data; or create new accounts with full user rights.

The security update addresses the vulnerability by correcting the input sanitization error to preclude unintended elevation.

Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute code in the security context of the affected service. The permissions available to the attacker would be limited to those granted to that service.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

factors.applicability: Microsoft states Customer Action Required Yes. Affected products are Windows 10 1607 to 22H2, Windows 11 23H2 to 26H2, and Windows Server 2016 to 2025.
factors.exploitability: AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N. Requires an authorized local account and winning a race condition (FAQ). No user interaction.
factors.remediation_context: Security updates per KB links. No vendor workaround. No local control maps to a removable feature.
factors.technical_impact: Use-after-free (CWE-416) with high confidentiality, integrity and availability impact. FAQ says code runs in the security context of the affected service, limited to that service's permissions.
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft exploitation_assessment less-likely, setting the Plausible floor. KEV false, exploitation detected false, publicly disclosed false, EPSS null. CISA-ADP SSVC exploitation none, technical impact total.
factors.uncertainty: The affected service's identity (and whether it runs as SYSTEM) is not stated, so the consequence is unknown. The FAQ says code execution, while the title is elevation of privilege.
factors.workload_context: Windows filtering platform on client and server endpoints across many versions. Local-to-SYSTEM is a challenge for Scheduled and is not established; the service-context limit is the only source bound.

risk_communication.summary: Important Windows Filtering Platform use-after-free elevation of privilege (CVSS 7.0, AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N). An authorized local account must win a race. Microsoft rates exploitation less likely, with no KEV, detected exploitation or EPSS.
risk_communication.why_this_action: Standard-remediation archetype at the Plausible floor, so Scheduled. Local-to-SYSTEM was challenged. The FAQ limits execution to the affected service's permissions, but whether that service runs as SYSTEM is not stated, so review is required. AC:H and the lack of exploitation evidence keep it from escalating.
risk_communication.control_limitations: Network controls do not apply to a local foothold. Race exploitation is not blocked by any mapped control. Least-privilege credit assumes the service account is restricted. No workaround exists.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could gain SYSTEM privileges.

factors.applicability: Microsoft Customer Action Required: Yes. Affected Windows 10 1607/1809/21H2/22H2, Windows 11 23H2/24H2/25H2/26H1/26H2 and Server 2016/2019/2022/2025, with per-product KB remediations.
factors.exploitability: Local authorized attacker must win a race (AC:H); PR:L, UI:N. The UAF is a memory-corruption prerequisite that Microsoft does not describe in detail.
factors.remediation_context: Security updates listed for all affected families. No workaround in source.
factors.technical_impact: Microsoft states SYSTEM privileges can be gained. Local-to-SYSTEM challenge: the impact is severe, but local foothold, AC:H and no exploitation observed keep Important Scheduled (Elevated needs More Likely; Critical needs a Critical rating).
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft less-likely (Plausible). KEV false; exploitation_detected false; publicly_disclosed false; EPSS null; CNA/ADP SSVC exploitation none.
factors.uncertainty: Publicly disclosed false does not prove no proof-of-concept exists. Target service and host population are not stated.
factors.workload_context: COM+ Event System Service on endpoints and servers. Multi-user or shared server hosts increase local-to-SYSTEM concentration; sizing is unknown from the source.

risk_communication.summary: Important local EoP to SYSTEM via a race-dependent use-after-free in the COM+ Event System Service, with an authorized local foothold required.
risk_communication.why_this_action: Standard remediation: Important with less-likely exploitation gives Plausible. SYSTEM impact was challenged; no source evidence of Elevated likelihood or exploitation supports Out-of-cycle.
risk_communication.control_limitations: Network and delivery controls do not apply to local access. Detection does not lower likelihood. Patch is the only source-backed fix.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

What privileges could an attacker gain by successfully exploiting this vulnerability?

An attacker could execute code with the permissions of another user on the affected system. This could give the attacker access to data and resources available to that user.

factors.applicability: Microsoft marks Customer Action Required: Yes for .NET 10 and 11 on Linux and Mac OS and for the Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Watch.Aspire package. The CNA record repeats these products and fixed versions.

factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft Exploitability Index is not published (unknown), so the Plausible not-published floor applies. KEV is false, exploitation detected is false, EPSS is null, and publicly disclosed is false. Microsoft E:U is recorded.
factors.uncertainty: The affected .NET feature and interface that the race runs against are not named. The privilege context of the target user is not stated, and Microsoft gives no exploitability rating.
factors.workload_context: Affects .NET on Linux and Mac OS, including the Aspire hot-reload package, which suggests developer and build hosts. Shared build or container hosts with several local users would raise cross-user concentration. The record does not state how such hosts are deployed.

risk_communication.summary: Important, CVSS 7.5 local elevation of privilege in .NET on Linux and Mac OS. It needs a local account and a race win. Plausible likelihood with Scheduled handling.

Cross-user access on shared developer or build hosts is the main concern that could justify faster handling.

An attacker with access to a local Windows account could bypass the isolation intended to restrict an affected ASP.NET Core service to its own account. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to access data or perform operations exposed by that service without the intended authorization.

notes.title: Description
notes.value: Heap-based buffer overflow in Microsoft Windows Codecs Library allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack vector is local (AV:L). Why does the CVE title indicate that this is a remote code execution?

The word Remote in the title refers to the location of the attacker. This type of exploit is sometimes referred to as Arbitrary Code Execution (ACE). The attack itself is carried out locally.

For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer.

According to the CVSS metric, the attack vector is local (AV:L). Why does the CVE title indicate that this is a remote code execution?

The word Remote in the title refers to the location of the attacker. This type of exploit is sometimes referred to as Arbitrary Code Execution (ACE). The attack itself is carried out locally.

How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker who can run a malicious application locally inside an AppContainer could submit specially crafted graphics data to the isolated graphics compilation service. title: Windows Installer Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability

mitigation_candidates.evidence: Public-ingress removal applies only to inbound service routes. The source establishes a local attack vector (AV:L) with an authorized local attacker and no listening service, so there is no public-ingress path to remove. Production vector guard also withholds effects because attack.vector is local.

Segmentation and ACLs constrain inbound, outbound or adjacent network entry. The established route is local with an existing authorized account and no network delivery, so no network-path restriction maps to the exploit. Production vector guard applies (attack.vector local).

The record names the Windows Installer component but no service or feature that the required operation depends on, and it provides no vendor disablement guidance. A bare component name is insufficient for ordinary benefit, so no credit is applied. Residual: the exploit path through Windows Installer remains unmitigated by this control.

The Microsoft guidance lists only security update remediations (KB5131085, KB5131090, KB5131096, KB5131080, KB5131077, KB5132061, KB5132043, KB5131087, KB5132059, KB5131291) and no workaround text. Update links are not mitigation credit, so no effect is applied.

An IPS or NGFW signature inspects network traffic. The source establishes a local double-free/race in Windows Installer with no network delivery or listening service, so there is no inspected path. Production vector guard applies (attack.vector local).

A WAF inspects inbound HTTP requests to a protected service. The source describes no web-facing route; the exploit path is local Windows Installer processing. Production vector guard applies (attack.vector local).

No configuration setting that removes an exploit prerequisite is named in the record. The stated prerequisites are a low-privilege authorized local account and a race condition (AC:H). No setting is established that eliminates either, so no credit is applied.

The source assumes an already valid authorized low-privilege account (PR:L). Strong authentication does not cure exploitation by an account that is already valid, so the existing foothold is not gated by any new authentication step.

PR:L is the generic low-privilege requirement and does not name a specific privilege that can be removed. Least privilege and PAM can reduce which accounts hold local access, but the exploit's privilege gain goes from a standard local account to SYSTEM, so limiting privileged groups does not remove the required privilege or contain SYSTEM once reached. No consequence credit is supported by the source.

Application control credit requires an established dependency on starting an untrusted executable or script. The record does not state the exploit delivery form (binary, script, or crafted installer package), so the dependency is not established and no credit is applied.
No ASR rule is established to map to a Windows Installer double free or TOCTOU race (CWE-415, CWE-367). Generic ASR presence is not a tested prevention rule, so no credit is applied.

Email and web filtering acts only on user-delivered content routes. The record describes an authorized local attacker and no mail or web delivery of attacker content, so the route does not exist in the source.
Protected View and macro hardening apply only to user-delivered Office content. The source describes a local Windows Installer elevation with no Office document route.
No tested EDR prevention rule for this specific double-free or race behavior is established by the record. Generic EDR presence does not earn credit, so no effect is applied.

EDR detection and response improves detection and response confidence for local privilege escalation. The rule for this control gives no likelihood credit, and it does not contain the SYSTEM consequence once reached, so no effect is applied.

Backups are a recovery control with no likelihood credit. The source's dominant consequence is SYSTEM-level confidentiality, integrity and availability impact (C:H/I:H/A:H), which backups do not contain or prevent. No consequence credit is supported.

Isolation constrains established network entry or delivery. Local entry alone receives no network credit, and the source establishes an authorized local account with no network route. Production vector guard applies (attack.vector local).

factors.applicability: MSRC marks Customer Action Required: Yes. Affected products are Windows 10 1607 through 22H2, Windows 11 23H2 through 26H2 (x64 and ARM64), and Windows Server 2016 through 2025 including Server Core. Per-product security updates are published (KB5131085, KB5131090, KB5131096, KB5131080, KB5131077, KB5132061, KB5132043, KB5131087, KB5132059, KB5131291). Customer action is therefore required and the no-customer-action archetype does not apply.
factors.exploitability: Local only (AV:L) with low privileges (PR:L) and no user interaction (UI:N). The MSRC FAQ states exploitation requires winning a race condition (AC:H). The CVSS exploit-maturity metric is E:U (unproven). CISA SSVC in the CNA ADP record gives automatable: no and exploitation: none. Reliability of the race is not characterised by the source.
factors.remediation_context: Security updates for each affected build are published by Microsoft. The record contains no vendor workaround and no service or feature disablement guidance, so the only documented remediation is patching. Source says Customer Action Required: Yes.
factors.technical_impact: A successful exploit yields SYSTEM privileges (MSRC FAQ). CVSS impact is High for confidentiality, integrity and availability with unchanged scope. CWE-415 (double free) and CWE-367 (TOCTOU race) are the stated weakness classes. CISA SSVC technical impact is total.
factors.threat_evidence: Microsoft Exploitability Index is less-likely, which sets a Plausible floor. KEV is false, exploitation_detected is false, publicly_disclosed is false, and CVSS E:U is unproven. EPSS is null (not provided) and is treated as unknown rather than low. The data is dated 2026-11-10, one day before this assessment.
factors.uncertainty: EPSS is absent, so no EPSS floor applies. The race is AC:H and its reliability is not characterised. The normalized temporal score is 6.1 while the copied base score is 7.0. Minor CNA CPE inconsistencies exist: Windows 11 23H2 appears twice, and one Windows 11 26H2 ARM64 criterion uses the application part 'a'. These do not change the MSRC product association or the baseline. The prerequisites for multi-user exploitation are not stated in the source.
factors.workload_context: Windows Installer is present on Windows endpoints and Windows Server hosts across all listed releases. Consequence is SYSTEM on any host where an authorized low-privilege account exists, which includes multi-user or shared-session hosts. Such hosts would widen cross-user and shared-secret consequences, but how many customer hosts are multi-user is unknown and is not assumed here. No workload-namespace tag is source-established, so none is emitted.

risk_communication.summary: Important, CVSS 7.0 local elevation-of-privilege in Windows Installer. An authorized low-privilege local user can reach SYSTEM by winning a race condition. Microsoft rates exploitation Less Likely, there is no KEV listing, no detected exploitation and no published EPSS, so the threat sits at the Plausible floor. The standard remediation archetype gives Scheduled.
risk_communication.why_this_action: The standard-remediation archetype applies because the vulnerability is Important, not Critical, and the likelihood is Plausible rather than Elevated, so the elevated-high-severity and critical archetypes do not select. Scheduled was challenged explicitly. Local-to-SYSTEM with total CISA technical impact and Windows Server exposure is a real concern, and multi-user or shared hosts could widen consequence. Against that, the entry requires an already-held authorized account, the exploit depends on an AC:H race, Microsoft gives E:U and SSVC gives automatable: no, and no exploitation signals exist. Those factors do not justify Out-of-cycle, so Scheduled stands. Operators with multi-user hosts can apply the security update in an earlier window, but that is an operator decision and not a baseline change.
risk_communication.control_limitations: All 17 controls are not applicable or unknown for the local route, or lack a tested mechanism, so no likelihood or consequence credit is applied. The network-only controls are withheld by the production vector guard because attack.vector is local. Backups, EDR and detection controls are recorded without credit. Only patching removes the vulnerable code path.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could gain ELEVATED privileges, which may allow them to perform actions beyond their original permissions.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires an attacker to win a race condition.

notes.value:
What privileges could be gained by an attacker who successfully exploited the vulnerability?

An attacker could use this vulnerability to elevate privileges from a Low Integrity Level in a contained ("sandboxed") execution environment to a Medium Integrity Level.

Please refer to AppContainer isolation and Mandatory Integrity Control for more information.

Successful exploitation requires the user's desktop to be unlocked and a suitable application window to be in the foreground. An attacker cannot reliably exploit this vulnerability when those conditions are not present.

According to the CVSS metric, the attack vector is local (AV:L). Why does the CVE title indicate that this is a remote code execution?

The word Remote in the title refers to the location of the attacker. This type of exploit is sometimes referred to as Arbitrary Code Execution (ACE). The attack itself is carried out locally. This means an attacker or victim needs to execute code from the local machine to exploit the vulnerability.

cna.description: HDF5 through 2.2.0 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability in H5L__extern_traverse() in src/H5Lexternal.c, the default traversal callback for external links. The callback locates the target file name and object path within the link’s user data using strlen() without validating the buffer against its stored size (udata_size, which was marked unused). A crafted HDF5 file containing an external link whose data is not NULL-terminated, or is too short to hold both strings, causes strlen() to read past the end of the udata heap buffer, and the derived object path pointer may also point outside the buffer. The overrun is unbounded and continues until a zero byte is found. The flaw is triggered when the malicious link is traversed, for example when opening an object through it. An attacker who can get a user or application to access a crafted file can cause a denial of service, and adjacent heap contents may be incorporated into the external file name or object path the library attempts to open.

notes.title: Description
notes.value: Improper control of generation of code ('code injection') in Windows PowerShell allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
How could an attacker exploit this vulnerability?

An attacker could convince a victim, or cause a victim-controlled automated process, to invoke Invoke-WebRequest against an attacker-controlled URL. By returning a specially crafted non-2xx HTML response, the attacker could cause Windows PowerShell to parse the response through MSHTML without displaying the security confirmation prompt, which could execute embedded script in the invoking PowerShell process.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack vector is local (AV:L). Why does the CVE title indicate that this is a remote code execution?

The word Remote in the title refers to the location of the attacker. This type of exploit is sometimes referred to as Arbitrary Code Execution (ACE). The attack itself is carried out locally.

For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer.

notes.value:
What kind of security feature could be bypassed by successfully exploiting this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could bypass Windows Defender Application Control and PowerShell Constrained Language Mode restrictions, allowing untrusted code to run with capabilities those protections are designed to block.

notes.title: Description
notes.value: Authentication bypass by capture-replay in SQL Server allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, the attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

The attacker must inject themselves into the logical network path between the target and the resource requested by the victim to read or modify network communications. This is called a machine-in-the-middle (MITM) attack.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
What type of information could be disclosed by this vulnerability?

An attacker who successfully exploited this vulnerability could obtain the encryption keys that protect data secured by Always Encrypted with secure enclaves. With access to these keys, the attacker could read the plaintext of the protected database columns, which may contain sensitive information.

notes.title: FAQ

I am running SQL Server on my system. What action do I need to take?

Update your relevant version of SQL Server using the applicable November 2026 security update listed below.

There are GDR and/or CU (Cumulative Update) updates offered for my version of SQL Server. How do I know which update to use?

  • First, determine your SQL Server version number. For more information, see Microsoft Knowledge Base Article 321185 - How to determine the version, edition, and update level of SQL Server and its components.
  • Second, locate the range containing your current version number in the following table. The corresponding update is the one you need to install.

What type of information could be disclosed by this vulnerability?

An attacker running in a restricted app environment could view portions of private image data previously handled by the thumbnail service outside that environment. The vulnerability does not provide unrestricted access to arbitrary files or credentials.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
According to the CVSS metric, attack complexity is high (AC:H). What does that mean for this vulnerability?

Successful exploitation requires the thumbnail service to have processed private image data and later reuse related memory for the attacker's thumbnail request. The attacker cannot assume that this combination of prior activity and memory reuse will occur.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

coredump: hold RCU while releasing parked threads

coredump_finish() releases the parked threads by clearing ->task in
their core_thread entry and calling wake_up_process() on each of them.
It does that without holding a reference on the task and without being
inside rcu.

But calling wake_up_process(task) without rcu here isn't safe. A parked
thread doesn't need that wakeup to leave. A spurious wakeup or a
preemption after the store is enough for the task to go away.

So if the coredump client is preempted between the store and
wake_up_process() the thread can exit and be freed in the meantime and
try_to_wake_up() takes pi_lock in freed memory.

Hold rcu across the loop.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

keys: Protect the type name while describing a key

keyctl_describe_key() must keep the key type's name alive until
kasprintf() has consumed it. The retained key reference keeps the key
and its description alive, but does not pin the module providing its
type. The name is passed to kasprintf() without holding key->sem.

kvasprintf() uses the saved name pointer in two formatting passes, with
a GFP_KERNEL allocation between them. With AF_RXRPC=m, a task that
passes View permission before type retirement can overlap a privileged
module unload in this order:

1. KEYCTL_DESCRIBE looks up the key, saves key->type->name in the
   kasprintf() arguments and completes the first formatting pass.
2. While the formatter is delayed before its second pass,
   af_rxrpc_exit() calls unregister_key_type(), which removes the type
   from the registry and waits for key_gc_keytype().
3. The collector takes key->sem for writing, retypes the retained key
   to key_type_dead and completes retirement. Unregistration and module
   exit return, allowing free_module() to release the type and name.
4. The formatter resumes its second pass and reads the saved name from
   released module storage, which can fault in string().

Hold key->sem for reading across kasprintf(). The collector then cannot
retype the key or complete retirement until both formatting passes have
finished. If retirement wins the lock first, formatting uses the core
key_type_dead name instead. Release the semaphore immediately after
kasprintf(), including on allocation failure, before copying to
userspace.

Oops report as below:

    BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: fffffbfff8054794
    #PF: supervisor read access in kernel mode
    #PF: error_code(0x0000) - not-present page
    RIP: 0010:string+0x23f/0x470
    Call Trace:

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tracing/histograms: Verify event_call identity when updating synth_event refcount

In event_hist_trigger_parse() and hist_unreg_all(), the histogram
registration and unregistration paths look up find_synth_event() using
trace_event_name(file->event_call) and adjust se->ref if a match is
found.

Because find_synth_event() only compares the event basename, registering
or removing a histogram on a non-synthetic trace event whose basename
matches a synthetic event erroneously modifies the synthetic event's
reference count.  If a histogram is registered on the non-synthetic
event before the synthetic event is created and removed afterwards,
se->ref is decremented without a matching increment, allowing the
synthetic event to be freed while an active histogram action still holds
a pointer to it.

Introduce find_synth_event_call() to verify that &se->call matches
file->event_call before adjusting se->ref.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tracing: Save the event file instead of the compatible histogram

create_field_var_hist() creates a histogram on the matched event to
supply a field variable, and records it on the target so it can be torn
down later:

	hist_data = find_compatible_hist(target_hist_data, file);
	...
	/* Save the compatible histogram information */
	var_hist->hist_data = hist_data;

hist_data is not the histogram it creates. It is one that was already
there, whose keys the new one copies. The saved pointer has a single
user, unregister_field_var_hists(), which runs when the target is
removed:

	file = hist_data->field_var_hists[i]->hist_data->event_file;

find_compatible_hist() matches on keys alone, so it can pick one with no
variables of its own. check_var_refs() then returns false and the user
can remove it while the target still points at it:

 BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in event_hist_trigger_free+0x2b2/0x320
 Read of size 8 at addr ffff8880093b90e0 by task init/1

 Freed by task 1:
  kfree+0x154/0x420
  event_hist_trigger_free+0x1d5/0x320
  event_hist_trigger_parse+0x35f3/0x69e0
  trigger_process_regex+0x1a6/0x250

Save the event file instead. It is all the dereference ever wanted, and
it does not go away when the user removes a trigger.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tracing: Reject incomplete event filter expressions

A non-empty expression normally finishes in predicate_parse()'s inner
loop, which resolves the pending logical operators before jumping to
finalization. If the input ends after an operator, possibly followed by
unary '!' tokens, the outer loop instead falls through with unresolved
operator state.

For example, "common_pid == 1 || common_pid == 2 &&" leaves
prog[0].target equal to -1. The second pass then reads prog[-1] before
the forward-jump check can reject it. Depending on adjacent slab
contents, it can also copy an out-of-bounds word into a branch target
that passes the forward-only check. A self-targeted perf tracepoint
counting event can reach this path through PERF_EVENT_IOC_SET_FILTER.

Reject the outer-loop fallthrough when a predicate has already been
parsed. This ensures that non-empty expressions only reach finalization
after the inner loop has resolved their operators. Keep the existing
no-filter error for input that has no predicates. Add a regression test
for trailing logical operators and unary negations.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tun: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach to an ownerless device

Twenty years ago I made creating a tuntap device require CAP_NET_ADMIN
in commit ca6bb5d7ab22 ("[NET]: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to create tuntap
devices.")

The idea was to allow the permissions on /dev/net/tun to be relaxed to
0666 and thus allow owners of tun devices assigned with TUNSETOWNER to
actually open it and get at their devices.

What we missed at the time was that persistent devices with *no* owner
were already essentially world-consumable, and anyone who could open
the device node could also attach to those.

Even then, using persistent devices with no explicitly set owner — on
the (false) presumption that CAP_NET_ADMIN would be required to open
them — wasn't an egregious userspace bug. There are cases where it does
make sense to separate the creation/configuration of the netdevice, from
the process which shovels packets into it.

Since then, TUNSETGROUP was added a year later in commit 8c644623fe7e
("[NET]: Allow group ownership of TUN/TAP devices."). Its commit message
noted that if both uid and gid are set, both have to match (in itself a
bizarre choice) — but still not that with *neither* set, no permission
at all was required.

Then in 2012 commit c8d68e6be1c3 ("tuntap: multiqueue support") allowed
new queues to be attached to a device from the moment of its creation,
with no way for userspace to close the race between creation and a
subsequent TUNSET{OWNER,GROUP}.

In 2024, commit 3ca459eaba1bf ("tun: fix group permission check") tried
to fix things to be saner: only require the user *or* the group to
match, in line with standard POSIX permissions, and require
CAP_NET_ADMIN if neither the user nor group authorised the access
(although it put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check first, and would wrongly have
reported the capability as having been used even when it was not).

That fix was reverted in commit a70c7b3cbc06 ("tun: revert fix group
permission check") due to allegedly causing a regression in an selinux
test suite which *expected* the attachment to succeed when authorised
by none of user, group, nor CAP_NET_ADMIN:
https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/CAFqZXNtkCBT4f+PwyVRmQGoT3p1eVa01fCG_aNtpt6dakXncUg@mail.gmail.com/

We should not break UAPI. But we don't have to consider an selinux test
case which deliberately exercises a security flaw to be UAPI worth
preserving either. To which end, I have fixed it in selinux-testsuite
commit b2f894f0016b ("tests/tun_tap: set an owner on the device for the
relabel tests").

So: fix the lack of CAP_NET_ADMIN check on devices which *haven't* been
assigned an owner or group, while leaving the weird tun ownership model
as it was (user *and* group have to match, if both are set). If someone
still wants to fix the latter (which wasn't actually the reason the
previous attempt was reverted), they can do it under separate cover.

Permit attaching to an existing device only if an owner and/or group was
set and the caller matches all that were set, or if the caller has
CAP_NET_ADMIN. The only behavioural change is that a device with no
owner or group now requires CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach — precisely the
loophole we want to close.

And put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check in the right place this time.

cna.description: Multiple Snowflake client drivers implementing the `authenticator=externalbrowser` single sign-on flow could have allowed an attacker to interfere with a user's login attempt through weaknesses in the local loopback callback listener used to receive the identity provider's response. The listener reflected an arbitrary request's Origin header into its CORS response headers and accepted the first token-bearing request it received during the login window without verifying a CSRF state value bound to that specific login attempt. An attacker able to reach the listener during an active login might have leveraged this to submit a forged callback response, causing the authentication attempt to fail. The fix is available in Snowflake Connector for Python 4.8.0, Snowflake Go Driver v2.3.0, Snowflake JDBC Driver 4.4.0 (including the snowflake-jdbc-fips and snowflake-jdbc-thin artifacts), Snowflake Node.js Driver 3.4.0, Snowflake Connector for .NET 6.3.0, Snowflake ODBC Driver 4.0.0, Snowflake PHP PDO Driver 4.3.0, and libsnowflakeclient 2.11.1. Go v1 users must migrate to the latest major version of the module. Users must manually upgrade.

cna.description:
CGI versions before 5.00 for Perl allow form fields to be smuggled past proxies and WAFs via multipart parsing that differs from the RFCs.

The multipart/form-data parser matches the boundary anywhere rather than at the start of a line, uses the boundary without its leading -- for some client-supplied User-Agent values, finds the Content-Disposition name and filename inside the quoted values of other parameters, and corrupts parts when the boundary nears the 4096-byte read size.

cna.description:
CGI versions before 5.00 for Perl allow HTTP header injection via entity decoding after the newline check in header and unchecked values in multipart_start and do_push.

An application that passes request data into these header values can be made to add headers or split the response.

notes.title: FAQ
notes.value:
Why is this Chrome CVE included in the Security Update Guide?

The vulnerability assigned to this CVE is in Chromium Open Source Software (OSS) which is consumed by Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based). It is being documented in the Security Update Guide to announce that the latest version of Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) is no longer vulnerable.

How can I see the version of the browser?

  2. Click on Help and Feedback
  3. Click on About Microsoft Edge

The vulnerability assigned to this CVE is in Chromium Open Source Software (OSS) which is consumed by Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based). It is being documented in the Security Update Guide to announce that the latest version of Microsoft Edge (Chromium-based) is no longer vulnerable.

How can I see the version of the browser?

  1. In your Microsoft Edge browser, click on the 3 dots (...) on the very right-hand side of the window
  2. Click on Help and Feedback
  3. Click on About Microsoft Edge

WAF inspects inbound requests to a protected service. The SMB server response flows outbound to the client, so no WAF path exists.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate the data area in SMB2_read()

SMB2_read() copies le32_to_cpu(rsp->DataLength) bytes from
(char *)rsp + rsp->DataOffset without checking that the range lies
within the response actually received. A READ response with
DataOffset == 0 makes smb2_get_data_area_len() zero the data length, so
smb2_check_message() accepts a frame as short as the fixed response,
while SMB2_read() still uses the server-supplied DataLength, capped only
by CIFS_MAX_MSGSIZE and the caller's length.

A malicious server can answer the synchronous read used by the
mfsymlinks (or SFU) symlink parser with an 81-byte READ response
carrying DataOffset 0 and DataLength 1067, making the client copy 1067
bytes from a 448-byte receive object (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds; up to
16 KiB in the general case).

Clamp a zero (or header-overlapping) DataOffset to read_rsp_size, as
handle_read_data() does for the asynchronous path, and reject the
response unless DataOffset + DataLength fits within rsp_iov.iov_len.
The SMB1 helper was fixed the same way in 5be5bdda5863.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reserve space for the UTF-16 terminator in stream info

smb_strtoUTF16() always writes a terminating zero UTF-16 unit after the
converted characters, but get_file_stream_info() budgets only
sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + streamlen * 2 for a stream entry
and sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + 7 * 2 for the trailing
"::$DATA" entry. When an entry exactly fills the 448-byte small response
buffer, the terminator is written two bytes past the allocation.

Reserve one extra UTF-16 unit in both budget checks. The terminator is
not part of the wire format, so the reported lengths are unchanged.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix fiemap wild read on empty truncated response

smb3_fiemap() treats -E2BIG from SMB2_ioctl() as a truncated range blob
and loops for the next chunk. If the server reports
STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW with OutputCount == 0, SMB2_ioctl() returns
-E2BIG with out_data == NULL and out_data_len == 0, and the existing
length checks accept the empty result. The loop then evaluates

	next = out_data[num - 1].file_offset + ...

with num == 0, reading 16 bytes before NULL.

Reject a truncated range blob that contains no range, so the resume
offset is never computed from an empty response. Also require the last
range in a truncated blob to advance the resume offset without
overflowing, and to stay within the requested range; a malicious or
broken server could otherwise make no progress or underflow len and loop
forever. Free the previous response buffer before retrying.

Reproduced on 6.6.87.2 with a malicious SMB2 server that answers
FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES with STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW and
OutputCount == 0; an FS_IOC_FIEMAP ioctl on the mount oopses in
cifs_fiemap() with CR2 = fffffffffffffff8. The code path is unchanged
on mainline.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reject short SESSION_SETUP responses

smb2_check_message() accepts frames shorter than struct smb2_pdu when
the SMB2 status is non-zero, before the minimum-PDU check added by
b4694f269e66d. A 64-byte STATUS_MORE_PROCESSING_REQUIRED SESSION_SETUP
response is therefore accepted even though it cannot contain the
SecurityBufferOffset and SecurityBufferLength fields.

The parser then reads those fields from stale bytes left in the reused
receive buffer by an earlier frame. With a long stale
SecurityBufferLength, decode_ntlmssp_challenge() copies up to about
64 KB from beyond the receive object and sends the data back to the
server in the NTLMv2 AUTHENTICATE target info.

Reject short MPR SESSION_SETUP responses before the short-error path,
and validate SecurityBufferOffset + SecurityBufferLength against the
received response length before decoding the challenge.

The ordering bypass is not new: the short-error early return predates
b4694f269e66d, and the unvalidated SecurityBufferLength read predates
the 2016 raw NTLMSSP split in 166cea4dc3a4, so all supported stable
trees are affected. Reproduced on 6.6.87.2; the path is unchanged on
mainline.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xen-netback: Fix UAF when reading statistics data

The network statistic data in the driver is protected by RCU.
Unfortunately when tearing down the queues after an error during
connecting to the frontend (e.g. due to illegal Xenstore data filled
in by the guest), the statistic data is being freed without
synchronizing the RCU state.  In case the data is being read via sysfs
in this phase, access to already freed memory or memory being in new
use is possible.

Fix that by calling synchronize_net() before freeing the queue data.

This is XSA-526 / CVE-2026-100080

From 3.10.0 until 4.2.1, filelock on Windows ignores the mode argument for WindowsFileLock files and the ReadWriteLock SQLite database. A lock created with mode=0o600 receives the parent directory's inheritable ACL because _open_non_reparse_fd and _nt_open do not create an owner-only security descriptor. cna.description:
In all prior released versions of FRRouting, the OSPFv3 (for IPv6) implementation does not check that OSPFv3 packets have a link-local source address and either a link-local destination or one of the protocol multicast destination groups.  This may enable malicious actors to establish OSPFv3 adjacencies from unexpectedly, distant IPv6 hosts. Proper usage of OSPFv3 authentication trailers (RFC 7166, as is best practice) prevents full exploitation of this issue, though may allow a malicious actor to waste CPU on authentication checks.


Note the linked PR #23935 is not sufficient to fix the issue as it only verifies the source address. It is the destination address that must be checked.


Required configuration: The OSPFv3 for IPv6 routing protocol must be running (ospf6d process) and in use (enabled globally with "router ospf6" and on specific interfaces with "ipv6 ospf6 area".)


Workaround: either:

  *  configure OSPFv3 authentication trailers ("ipv6 ospf6 authentication")
  *  or ensure through firewall configuration that only packets with link-local or multicast destination addresses are accepted on input for IPv6 protocol 89 (OSPF). Note that checking the source address is insufficient, as some routers may (unexpectedly) forward packets with global-scoped IPv6 destination addresses even if they have link-local source addresses.

cna.description: HDF5 through 2.2.0 contains an uncontrolled recursion vulnerability in H5B__iterate_helper() in src/H5B.c. When iterating a version 1 B-tree, the function does not verify that a child node’s level matches the expected level. That check is performed only in H5B__cache_deserialize() when a node is first loaded into the metadata cache. A crafted HDF5 file whose B-tree child pointer refers back to a node already in the cache, such as a node that points to itself, bypasses the check and causes unbounded recursion, leading to stack exhaustion and a crash. This can be triggered by calling H5Gget_info() or H5Gget_num_objs() on a group in the crafted file, which reaches H5B_iterate() through H5G__obj_info() and H5G__stab_count(). An attacker who can get a user or application to open a malicious file can cause a denial of service.

cna.description: HDF5 through 2.2.0 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in H5Z__filter_szip() in src/H5Zszip.c. When decoding a szip-compressed chunk, the function subtracts the 4-byte uncompressed-length header from the chunk length without first verifying that the chunk is at least 4 bytes long. A truncated or corrupted chunk shorter than the header causes the length calculation to wrap around to a very large value, and the decompressor reads far past the end of the chunk buffer. An attacker who can get a user or application to read a dataset from a crafted HDF5 file can cause a denial of service. Only builds with szip support (libaec or the szip library) are affected.

cna.description: HDF5 through 2.2.0 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability in H5O__chunk_deserialize() in src/H5Ocache.c. When decoding object header messages, the declared message size is checked against the end of the chunk image before the remainder of the message header (flags, and for version 2 object headers, the optional creation index) has been decoded. Because the message body begins after these fields, a message can start up to four bytes further into the chunk than the size check accounts for. A crafted HDF5 file can declare a message size that passes the check but extends past the end of the chunk image, causing the message’s decode callback, for example H5O__mtime_new_decode() in src/H5Omtime.c, to read beyond the heap allocation. The flaw is reachable during H5Fopen() on a crafted file. An attacker who can get a user or application to open a malicious file can cause a denial of service or limited disclosure of process memory.

cna.description: HDF5 through 2.2.0 contains a NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in H5HL_unprotect() in src/H5HL.c. H5HL_protect() pins a single metadata cache entry for a local heap, either the heap prefix or the separate data block, and H5HL_unprotect() unpins it on the final unprotect. When the metadata cache destroys a corrupted local heap entry, H5HL__prfx_dest() unlinks it from the heap by setting heap->prfx or heap->dblk to NULL. A crafted HDF5 file can therefore reach H5HL_unprotect() with no cached object to unpin, and the function passes the NULL pointer to H5AC_unpin_entry(). This causes an assertion failure in debug builds and a NULL pointer dereference and crash in release builds. An attacker who can get a user or application to open and traverse a malicious file can cause a denial of service.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ftrace: Initialize modname and offset in print_rec()

print_rec() leaves 'modname' and 'offset' uninitialized and
kallsyms_lookup() only sets them on success. When the lookup fails like
when a module is being loaded or unloaded, 'modname' holds a garbage
value, passes the 'if (modname)' check, and is dereferenced by
seq_printf().

  Oops: general protection fault
  RIP: 0010:string+0x48/0xe0
  Call Trace:
   vsnprintf+0x1f5/0x650
   seq_printf+0x8e/0xb0
   print_rec+0x6c/0xc0
   t_show+0x4c/0x440
   seq_read_iter+0x119/0x480

This can be triggered by reading available_filter_functions while a
module is being loaded or unloaded.

Initialize both variables so a failed lookup skips the module name.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

asymmetric_keys: reject trust keys without IDs

The PKCS#8 parser deliberately leaves the asym_key_ids payload slot
empty. key_or_keyring_common() unconditionally dereferences that slot
when a PKCS#8 key is supplied to a key_or_keyring restriction. Both the
plain and :chain forms reach this branch, allowing an unprivileged caller
to trigger a NULL pointer dereference through KEYCTL_RESTRICT_KEYRING
followed by add_key().

 Oops: general protection fault, probably for non-canonical address 0xdffffc0000000000
 KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
 RIP: 0010:key_or_keyring_common (crypto/asymmetric_keys/restrict.c:205 crypto/asymmetric_keys/restrict.c:279)
 Call Trace:
  <TASK>
  __key_create_or_update (security/keys/key.c:884)
  key_create_or_update (security/keys/key.c:1021)
  __do_sys_add_key (security/keys/keyctl.c:134)
  do_syscall_64 (arch/x86/entry/common.c:52 arch/x86/entry/common.c:83)
  entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe (arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S:130)
  </TASK>
 Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Reject an asymmetric restriction key without key IDs. A PKCS#8 private
key cannot identify the signer of a candidate certificate and is not a
valid trust anchor.

cna.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

keys: Protect the read method check against type removal

keyctl_read_key() checks key->type->read without holding key->sem.
A reference keeps the key alive, but does not pin the module containing
its type. A surviving RxRPC key can therefore be read while AF_RXRPC
is being unloaded:

  KEYCTL_READ task                    Module unload and key GC
  ----------------                   ------------------------
  lookup_user_key()
  permission / possession checks
  load key->type
                                     af_rxrpc_exit()
                                       unregister_key_type()
                                         GC: down_write(key->sem)
                                         GC: retype to key_type_dead
                                         GC: up_write(key->sem)
                                       unregister_key_type() returns
                                     free_module()
  read saved type's read member

The final access can read freed module storage. The read invocation in
__keyctl_read_key() is already protected by key->sem, but the earlier
method check is outside that critical section.

Move the method check into __keyctl_read_key(), after key_validate() and
under its existing read hold on key->sem. The check and invocation then
use the same protected type for length queries and every read retry.
The GC cannot retype the key until the semaphore is released, and type
unregistration waits for that GC pass before the module can be freed.

Return -EOPNOTSUPP when validation succeeds and the type has no read
method. A temporary buffer may now be allocated before this result;
allocation and copying to userspace remain outside the semaphore.
